newsitem.title: HUNGARY: ADtranz meets expectations with early profit.
newsitem.headline: ADtranz meets expectations with early profit.

text.p: ADtranz, the world's largest maker of trains and railroad equipment, said Wednesday it made a 21 million ECU ($24.2 million) pre-tax profit in its first year of business.

ADtranz was formed Jan. 1, 1996, when industrial giants Daimler-Benz AG and ABB Asea Brown Boveri Ltd merged their rail units into a single Berlin-based company, transforming at a stroke the face of the rail equipment industry.

"ADtranz is on the right track," Chief Executive Kaare Vagner told reporters. "The full scope of benefits targeted by merging the respective railway activities of Daimler-Benz and ABB into the ADtranz group will become apparent in 1998."

The Danish chairman, in Budapest for a meeting of senior executives, noted that orders last year did not live up to expectations and that the global rail market may not grow as quickly as expected, but that the company was where he had hoped it would be financially.
ADtranz reported 1996 sales of 3.196 billion ECU ($3.68 billion) and operating profit after depreciation of 129 million ECU ($149 million).
"This is not bad for a company that is only one year old," Vagner said.
He said he is upbeat about this year and next, predicting sales of 3.7 billion ECU ($4.3 billion) in 1997 and a "much higher" profit.
ADtranz's safe birth comes as good news for its two parents, who had hoped to improve their rail business by combining forces in an attempt to cut overhead and take advantage of economies of scale.

Vagner said he was especially hopeful about business in Asia, where crowded cities are scrambling to develop mass transit systems, and in the United Kingdom, which appears to be showing an appetite for rolling stock after years of making do with old equipment.

ADtranz, short for ABB Daimler-Benz Transportation GmbH, holds an estimated 12 percent of the world rail equipment market, followed by Germany's Siemens AG and a joint venture between France's Alcatel Alsthom and General Electric Co.
